paragraphs.source_en: After this, Lhazang Khan recognized the incarnate lama Ngawang Yeshe Gyatso, born in 1686, the Fire Tiger year of the Tibetan calendar, as the Sixth Dalai Lama, and brought him to the Potala Palace for enthronement; he remained in that position for eleven years. However, the monks and laypeople of Tibet did not acknowledge him as the reincarnated child of the Dalai Lama. After Pekar Dzinpa Yeshe Gyatso was enthroned, Lhazang Khan submitted a memorial to the Kangxi Emperor, asking the emperor to recognize him as the Dalai Lama and to bestow a golden seal. The emperor granted the request and bestowed a golden seal; the inscription, originally “Seal of the Imperially Enfeoffed Sixth Dalai Lama,” was altered to “Seal Imperially Bestowed upon the Sixth Dalai Lama.” (Register of Seals, p. 11)

paragraphs.source_en: The most widely circulated account is the version found in the “secret biography,” The Sound of the Pipa. “In the Fire Pig year, when the Dharma King, that is, Tsangyang Gyatso, was twenty-five, he was invited to travel to the interior.” “As the party proceeded in stages to Dongru Tsona, the emperor’s edict was severe; when everyone heard the command, they were terrified to the utmost. They feared that their lives could not be saved, and they had no good plan with which to respond. Thereupon, with one voice, they pleaded with me, Tsangyang Gyatso: ‘You have already gained mastery over yourself; you can manifest the appearance of passing into immortality, or hide away your bodily form. If you do not do this, then we are certain to be beheaded.’ They begged again and again. Tsangyang Gyatso was filled with boundless sorrow; after taking leave, he suddenly set out, going toward the southeast... After that, he passed through Dartsedo and went to Mount Emei and other places in the interior to make pilgrimages and worship the Buddha. Then he wandered through Ü and Tsang, India, Nepal, Gansu, Mount Wutai, Qinghai, Mongolia, and other places, preaching scriptures and expounding the Dharma, forming many good karmic ties, and creating innumerable subtle and wondrous deeds.

paragraphs.source_en: When the Cultural Revolution began in 1966, rebels burst into the Southern Monastery, smashed the spirit stupa of the Sixth Dalai Lama, forced the monks themselves to destroy the mummified body of the Sixth Dalai Lama, and burned large numbers of Buddhist images and scriptures. The few lamas who had guarded the monastery were denounced as “monsters and demons” and driven out; some homeless monks were expelled to nearby production brigades and communes. In the early 1970s, all the halls and buildings of the Southern Monastery were dismantled, the timber was used for other purposes, and the property was sold off cheaply by the relevant authorities. The Southern Monastery became a field of ruins.

At the same time, he secretly sent people everywhere to search for the reincarnated child of the Fifth Dalai Lama.

paragraphs.source_en: In the Tsona area of Shannan, they found a clever and charming child, identified him as the reincarnation of the Fifth Dalai Lama, and brought him to Tsona Castle to be quietly supported and raised. When he was fifteen, he was enthroned in the great hall of the Potala Palace; this was the Sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso. Tsangyang Gyatso did not like being worshipfully kept in the Potala Palace like a god or Buddha. The endless chanting and ritual worship from morning to night made him deeply weary, so he put on layman’s clothes, wore a long wig, took the assumed name Tangsang Wangbu, and slipped away to Lhasa’s Barkhor Street or to the Snow Village beneath the Potala Palace to seek out male and female friends, play, and enjoy the pleasures of worldly life. paragraphs.source_en: On a small island in the lake of the gardens behind the Potala Palace, Tsangyang Gyatso built an exquisite pavilion called the Dragon King Pool. There he gathered young men and women from the city of Lhasa to sing, dance, drink, and make merry together. Tsangyang Gyatso composed many love songs for everyone to sing, and these songs quickly spread throughout Tibet and were much loved by the people. At the Dragon King Pool, Tsangyang Gyatso came to know a girl from Chongye named Dawa Zhuoma. Dawa Zhuoma was beautiful in appearance, gentle in temperament, and sweet of voice; her pair of black, bright eyes were like newly made grape wine, enough to intoxicate a person with a single glance. Tsangyang Gyatso and she knew and loved one another deeply, as though each were the other’s shadow; by day they sang, danced, wandered, and played together, and at night they often met in secret. Tsangyang Gyatso loved Dawa Zhuoma greatly, believing her to be a gift from the deities and a bond from a former life; he wrote the following song to express his feelings:

units.source_en: On a small island in the lake of the gardens behind the Potala Palace, Tsangyang Gyatso built an exquisite pavilion called the Dragon King Pool. There he gathered young men and women from the city of Lhasa to sing, dance, drink, and make merry together. Tsangyang Gyatso composed many love songs for everyone to sing, and these songs quickly spread throughout Tibet and were much loved by the people.
